subChunks.title: Complex Animation Orchestration
subChunks.hookHtml: Simple animations — a fade in, a scale on hover, a spinning loader — are solved by Tailwind's built-in utilities. Complex animation orchestration — staggered list entrances, sequenced multi-step transitions, scroll-triggered reveals, and coordinated component choreography — requires combining Tailwind's animation system with CSS custom properties, intersection observers, and JavaScript-driven timing. This lesson covers the patterns that make production-grade animation feel intentional.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Sable the Illuminator: "Good animation is barely noticeable. Great animation is completely invisible — it just makes the interface feel alive and responsive. You are not making fireworks. You are making the interface breathe."

Stagger pattern using CSS custom properties

/* The CSS-only stagger: use CSS custom property for delay */
@keyframes fade-up {
  from { opacity: 0; transform: translateY(12px); }
  to   { opacity: 1; transform: translateY(0); }
}

/* In the component: each item sets its own --delay */
<ul>
  {items.map((item, i) => (
    <li
      key={item.id}
      style={{ '--delay': `${i * 60}ms` } as React.CSSProperties}
      className="animate-fade-up [animation-delay:var(--delay)] [animation-fill-mode:both]"
    >
      {item.name}
    </li>
  ))}
</ul>

/* animation-fill-mode: both:
   - backwards: applies from-keyframe styles before animation starts
   - forwards: holds final keyframe after animation ends
   - both: both — prevents the element from flashing to full opacity before its delay */

Scroll-triggered animation with Intersection Observer

/* CSS: hidden until revealed */
.reveal {
  opacity: 0;
  transform: translateY(20px);
  transition: opacity 0.5s ease, transform 0.5s ease;
}
.reveal.is-visible {
  opacity: 1;
  transform: translateY(0);
}

/* JavaScript: Intersection Observer triggers the class */
'use client';
import { useEffect, useRef } from 'react';

export function Reveal({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  const ref = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    const observer = new IntersectionObserver(
      ([entry]) => { if (entry.isIntersecting) ref.current?.classList.add('is-visible'); },
      { threshold: 0.1 }
    );
    if (ref.current) observer.observe(ref.current);
    return () => observer.disconnect();
  }, []);

  return <div ref={ref} className="reveal">{children}</div>;
}

Multi-step transition via state machine

'use client';
import { useState } from 'react';

type State = 'idle' | 'loading' | 'success' | 'error';

const stateClasses: Record<State, string> = {
  idle:    'bg-indigo-600 text-white',
  loading: 'bg-indigo-400 text-white cursor-wait',
  success: 'bg-emerald-600 text-white',
  error:   'bg-red-600 text-white',
} satisfies Record<State, string>;

export function AsyncButton({ onClick }: { onClick: () => Promise<void> }) {
  const [state, setState] = useState<State>('idle');

  const handleClick = async () => {
    setState('loading');
    try {
      await onClick();
      setState('success');
      setTimeout(() => setState('idle'), 2000);
    } catch {
      setState('error');
      setTimeout(() => setState('idle'), 3000);
    }
  };

  return (
    <button
      onClick={handleClick}
      className={`${stateClasses[state]} px-6 py-2 rounded-lg font-semibold
                  transition-colors duration-300 motion-reduce:transition-none`}
    >
      {{ idle: 'Submit', loading: 'Saving…', success: '✓ Saved', error: '✗ Error' }[state]}
    </button>
  );
}

The FLIP animation technique with Tailwind

/* FLIP: First Last Invert Play */
/* Used for animating layout changes (reordering, expanding) */

/* 1. Record element's position (First) */
const first = element.getBoundingClientRect();

/* 2. Apply the change (move element in DOM) */
list.prepend(element);

/* 3. Record new position (Last) */
const last = element.getBoundingClientRect();

/* 4. Invert the change (move element back visually) */
const dx = first.left - last.left;
const dy = first.top - last.top;
element.style.transform = `translate(${dx}px, ${dy}px)`;

/* 5. Play (animate to natural position) */
requestAnimationFrame(() => {
  element.classList.add('transition-transform', 'duration-300');
  element.style.transform = '';
});

Sable: "The golden rule: animate transform and opacity only. These are the only properties the browser can animate on the compositor thread — no layout, no paint, just the GPU. Any other property (width, height, padding, color) triggers layout or paint on the main thread, causing jank. Transform and opacity. That is the list."

storyBeats.speaker: Sable the Illuminator
storyBeats.text: Animate only transform and opacity. These two properties are handled by the compositor thread — no layout recalculation, no paint, pure GPU. Everything else causes jank. The entire science of smooth animation reduces to: transform and opacity, nothing else.

subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Build a scroll-triggered reveal page from scratch with at least 4 sections that fade in as they enter the viewport. Each section should use the CSS reveal/is-visible pattern. Include: a hero section, a features grid, a testimonial, and a CTA. Include the JavaScript Intersection Observer setup as an HTML comment block explaining the pattern. Also build a multi-step button (idle → loading → success → error) with state-machine class switching. No starter code.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain why animating only transform and opacity is the golden rule of smooth web animation. What happens to the browser's render pipeline when you animate a property like width or background-color instead? Then explain the CSS custom property stagger pattern — why use --delay as a CSS variable instead of computing animation-delay classes in JavaScript?

questions.prompt: Why should animations only use transform and opacity properties?
options: They are the only properties animated on the compositor thread — no layout or paint recalculation, enabling smooth 60fps animation without main thread jank
They are the only properties Tailwind's animation utilities support
Other properties cannot be keyframed in CSS
Transform and opacity have better browser support than other animatable properties
questions.answer: They are the only properties animated on the compositor thread — no layout or paint recalculation, enabling smooth 60fps animation without main thread jank
questions.explanation: The browser render pipeline has three phases: layout, paint, and composite. Animating transform or opacity only requires the composite step — the browser can hand this off to the GPU without recalculating layout or repainting pixels. Animating width, height, padding, margin, or background-color triggers layout and/or paint on every frame, which is expensive and causes dropped frames (jank) especially on lower-end devices.

questions.prompt: A list of 8 items should enter the screen with a 60ms stagger (item 0 at 0ms, item 1 at 60ms, etc.). Which implementation is most maintainable?
options: Set --delay CSS variable via inline style on each item and reference it in the Tailwind class: style={{ '--delay': `${i*60}ms` }} className="[animation-delay:var(--delay)]"
Create 8 separate Tailwind classes: delay-0, delay-60, delay-120, delay-180, delay-240, delay-300, delay-360, delay-420
Use JavaScript setTimeout to add an animate-enter class to each item after the stagger delay
Set animation-delay directly via inline style: style={{ animationDelay: `${i*60}ms` }}
questions.answer: Set --delay CSS variable via inline style on each item and reference it in the Tailwind class: style={{ '--delay': `${i*60}ms` }} className="[animation-delay:var(--delay)]"
questions.explanation: The CSS custom property pattern is most maintainable because: (1) the animation class string is identical for all items — no dynamic class generation that breaks the JIT scanner; (2) the delay is data (a number), not a class name — it doesn't need to exist in source files for the JIT to generate; (3) changing the stagger timing only requires changing the multiply factor, not a class list. Direct inline style (answer D) also works, but the CSS variable approach is preferred when the delay drives multiple CSS properties.

questions.prompt: A hero section uses a multi-step entrance: the background fades in (0ms), the heading slides up (200ms), the body text fades in (400ms), and the CTA scales in (600ms). A colleague suggests using animation-delay on each element with animate-* classes. A senior engineer pushes back and says this approach has a critical visual bug. What is it?
options: Without animation-fill-mode: both (or backwards), elements flash to their final visible state before their delay expires — the heading appears at full opacity before 200ms, then disappears, then animates in
Multiple animated elements on the same page conflict with each other — only one animation can run at a time per page
animate-* classes cannot be combined with animation-delay on the same element
The approach is correct — there is no bug
questions.answer: Without animation-fill-mode: both (or backwards), elements flash to their final visible state before their delay expires — the heading appears at full opacity before 200ms, then disappears, then animates in
questions.explanation: By default, animation-fill-mode is none — the element renders in its normal state during the delay period, then jumps to the from-keyframe when the animation starts. For a fade-up animation (from: opacity 0, translateY 12px), without fill-mode the element is visible during the delay, invisible at 200ms, then fades in. The fix is [animation-fill-mode:both] (or at minimum 'backwards') which applies the from-keyframe state during the delay — the element is invisible from the start and only becomes visible when its animation plays.
